To achieve this, we introduce a new method of verification, based on a conventional approach, and show that it allows for the confirmation of a quantum computation, even with the constraints of limited visibility, by utilizing a simple classical channel. Furthermore, we investigate the optimal strategy for the verifier, demonstrating that an efficient classical channel can successfully verify the quantum computation, provided it is received within two rounds of communication.

This paper proposes an innovative framework for Blockchain technology, suitable for Internet of Things applications in complex systems, requiring high reliability, security and transparency. The proposed solution addresses the typical Blockchain challenges of slow transaction verification by integrating support for Oracles and Intelligent Contracts. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application in a food supply chain network, where a Blockchain-based solution is developed to optimize the transaction verification process and enhance security. The proposed framework's performance is evaluated using a Raspberry Pi-based IoT device and a Bitcoin Blockchain, showing a significant improvement in transaction processing speed compared to traditional Blockchain methods.

Artificial intelligence has shown potential in classifying cell types using shape features, but its applications in generating cell shapes are limited. Current deep learning-based methods struggle to handle complex cell morphology, often focusing on simplified representations. In this study, we investigate the use of implicit neural representations to model intricate cell shapes, starting from a basic function and modifying it to capture morphological details. Our approach enables accurate modeling and semi-supervised generation of complex cell shapes, paving the way for de novo cell creation. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on two types of cells, achieving state-of-the-art results in shape reconstruction and outperforming existing generative techniques in our controlled experiments.

The widespread adoption of digital document sharing has significantly altered how information is disseminated, offering greater accessibility than traditional print methods. Nevertheless, individuals facing visual impairments still encounter substantial hurdles in navigating digital documents. This research aims to highlight the critical importance of digital document accessibility and explore recent advancements in solving related problems, particularly in data extraction tasks.

Recent pretraining methods for NLP, such as BERT and RoBERTa, have achieved impressive results across various tasks. Nonetheless, their reliance on left-to-right pretraining and masking techniques like MLM and NLML restricts their ability to capture contextual dependencies. To overcome this limitation, we present XLNet, a universally pretrained language model that leverages autoregressive decomposition of bidirectional language modeling. This innovative approach permits the model to consider all factors in the context when predicting each word, thereby avoiding conflicts between masking and autoregressive objectives. Moreover, XLNet incorporates additional advancements, including permutation filling objectives and balanced training objectives. Experimental evaluations on multiple tasks demonstrate XLNet's superiority over BERT and RoBERTa, achieving up to 2.2 points higher maximum F1 score on the GLUE benchmark.

The detection of biomarkers in exoplanet atmospheres through transit spectroscopy may be hindered by stellar activity, which can be reduced using high-resolution spectroscopy. We investigated the impact of stellar behavior on low-resolution spectroscopy, examined techniques to minimize its effects, and compared the efficiency of high-resolution and low-resolution spectroscopy in transit spectroscopy. We simulated the transit spectra of a hypothetical exoplanet around an active star using synthetic data and real-world GJ 667 Cf, and found that stellar activity can be mistaken for atmospheric features in low-resolution spectroscopy. High-resolution spectroscopy can identify the presence of activity markers in the star's spectrum, allowing for the separation of stellar and planetary signals. However, high-resolution spectroscopy may not always provide a clear separation of signals in cases of highly active stars, and is not a suitable replacement for low-resolution spectroscopy.

We establish a theoretical framework for the existence of constant curvature metrics on Riemann surfaces with singularities, drawing inspiration from the ideas of Madsen and Weiss who proved the Sullivan--Taylor conjecture for mapping spaces, and building upon the earlier work of Taylor and the first author who extended the Graves--Morris theorem to compact manifolds.

Research on swimming dynamics of low Reynolds forces is extensive, yet the dynamics of high-speed, three-dimensional (3D) active swimmers remain poorly understood. This study reveals the 3D agility of centipedes, specifically how they use their legs to propel themselves forward in both air and on the water's surface. High-speed cameras provided detailed insights into the centipedes' leg movements, and their body movements were observed to be closely linked. When moving at high speeds, the centipedes' leg movements were found to be synchronized, and their body undulations were directed along the line of propulsion, allowing them to maintain direction and generate forward thrust. This 3D swimming motion was found to be similar to that of fish, and the centipedes' ability to move quickly and efficiently in both air and water environments makes them well-suited to their habitat, likely enabling them to catch prey and escape predators with ease.

Tsunamis that result from asteroid impacts can have devastating effects on planetary defense and the environment. Understanding how these events unfold is crucial, so scientists have developed complex models to study tsunami simulations on other planets. However, these models are often limited by their high computational cost, which makes them impractical for certain scenarios. To address this issue, we have developed a new method that uses a simplified approach to simulate tsunami propagation on celestial bodies with complex internal structures. Our approach combines finite element analysis with a simplified model of diffusive processes and can be used to simulate various types of fluids, such as water or air. We have tested our method by simulating tsunami propagation on Mars and found that it accurately captures the key features of these events. Our results suggest that asteroid impacts can generate tsunamis that travel at incredible speeds on Mars, reaching distances of over 1000 km in a matter of hours. Our method is highly flexible and can be used to simulate a wide range of scenarios, from the impact of small meteorites to the collision of large asteroids.

A subset of luminous infrared galaxies consists of star-forming galaxies that are optically dim and lack a significant active galactic nucleus component. These galaxies are of great interest as they are thought to be the primary contributors to star formation at intermediate redshifts. A study utilizing early JWST data has revealed the characteristics of these galaxies, which are found to be highly dusty and heavily obscured. A separate analysis using the BAYESPECTRES code has simulated the infrared spectra of these galaxies, which are primarily driven by star-forming galaxies. A significant finding is that these galaxies are experiencing intense bursts of star formation, with average rates exceeding 100 times the typical rates in the Milky Way. A notable discovery is the presence of a substantial number of galaxies with star formation rates exceeding 1000 solar masses per year, which are thought to be the result of mergers of massive galaxies. A comparison with a photometric catalog of sub-millimeter galaxies has revealed that these galaxies are likely to be the counterparts to two-thirds of the sources in the COSMOS2020 catalog, which are thought to be the primary targets for future galaxy evolution studies.

A modified version of the seven-dimensional curvature term in the Einstein-Hilbert action is introduced, incorporating an additional geometrical term. This term is derived from a three-dimensional cross-section of a four-dimensional manifold, specifically its self-dual curvature tensor. By doing so, the cross-section's geometric structure is emulated. The focus is on classical field equations, for which an energy-momentum tensor expression is also obtained.

This research examines the scenario where a disc is blocked and unable to move in a two-dimensional environment with a frictionless surface, and we derive an exact solution for the disc's motion when it is pushed against another disc, which in turn is blocked and positioned off-center. We also investigate the exchange of Bessel indices between the two discs. Furthermore, we extend our findings to a channel-like setup where multiple discs are placed in a row and explore the behavior of each disc as it is pushed into the channel, documenting the exchange of Bessel indices between adjacent discs in alternating sequences.

Recent studies have highlighted the importance of the Equatorial Pacific in shaping large-scale climate patterns, particularly those related to El Ni\~no-Southern Oscillation (ENSO). This research examines how two distinct types of ENSO phenomena, known as PM-normalized ENSO-1&2 and Elevation ENSO, affect precipitation patterns around the world. By utilizing a global atmospheric reanalysis dataset and analyzing it in conjunction with specific trace patterns, we found that these two ENSO varieties exhibit unique and distinct impacts on global precipitation. While PM-normalized ENSO-1&2 is primarily linked to significant changes in low-elevation areas, Elevation ENSO is found to have a more pronounced effect on elevated regions. This distinction is particularly evident when considering high-resolution topographic data. This research provides new insights into how different ENSO varieties influence various global climate phenomena, such as atmospheric circulation, precipitation, and snowpack variations.

To examine the phenomenon of non-affine growth in a mixture of colloidal spheres and polyethylene glycol in brine, we employed dynamic light scattering and measured the intensity of scattered light over time. By analyzing the intensity patterns, we calculated a power-law exponent, $\alpha$, and found that it correlates with Elongation indices of non-affine growth particles. Furthermore, our research indicates that larger particles tend to exhibit steeper power-law patterns. We found that particles with higher Elongation indices tend to have higher values of $\alpha$. We also discovered that the intensity patterns can be described using both fractal and power-law models, but the power-law model provides a more accurate fit for longer observation times.

This research paper explores single-species demographic models within an age-based framework, accounting for a population model with behavioral influences in an environment that has been polluted. We establish an integral equation to model population dynamics and prove the existence and uniqueness of a positive steady-state solution under specific conditions. Our analysis also shows that the population model responds in certain ways to environmental changes and pollution, specifically in the Cantor set $\left\{\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{5},\frac{4}{5}\right\}$. Our findings are further supported by numerical simulations, which demonstrate the model's behavior under different scenarios.

We examine the computational properties of specific finite-hypersequent effectiveness requirements in a group of Weakening and Reduction hypersequent substructural logics. These properties are relevant to the study of hypersequent effectivity, a key concept in the development of hypersequent calculi for substructural logics. We investigate the membership in the class $\mathsf{P}$ of problems solvable in polynomial time and the class $\mathsf{NP}$
of problems solvable through non-deterministic polynomial time, as well as the decidability of a particular class of problems. Our findings reveal that each of the considered properties is either decidable or can be determined via a reduction to a known $\mathsf{P}$-complete language. We also establish that the specific computational properties of a particular language, $\mathsf{FDE}^{\bot}$, cannot be fully determined through this method, as they are instead resolved via a reduction to the $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete language emptiness problem for multihead automata.

In the field of data classification, many current methods rely on a fixed-dimensional vector space to represent data. However, this traditional approach has a limitation in terms of capacity, as it can only effectively model data in a fixed-dimensional space. To address this issue, a new method called HyperExpan has been developed to significantly increase the classification capacity of traditional approaches. HyperExpan utilizes a hyperbolic neural network to learn an expanding representation of data, allowing it to effectively model complex data in a higher-dimensional space while maintaining efficiency. The hyperbolic neural network is trained using a unique TripletExpan loss function that measures the distance between different data classes in a directed graph. The effectiveness of HyperExpan has been demonstrated through comprehensive testing on various synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing its ability to significantly improve classification performance on graphs with hierarchical structures.

The effect of varying electric fields on the binding energies of molecular pairs in the S66 dataset has been studied using a multigrid Monte Carlo method to obtain interaction energies calculated to chemical accuracy. It was discovered that a consistent energy pattern across the dataset is achieved when the axis of the electric field is aligned with the symmetry axis of the dimer. The energy contributions due to electric field effects were found to be substantial in some cases, with a notable trend of positive and negative interaction energies being observed in response to the field strength. The findings also highlight the importance of considering multiple a posteriori estimates to evaluate the uncertainty in the interaction energies. The results demonstrate the capability of energy decomposition analysis to distinguish between the dominant energy contributions in non-covalent interactions, with the effect of the electric field being a significant factor in most cases. The study further emphasizes the importance of considering the influence of varying electric field conditions in the study of molecular interactions, particularly in the context of biological systems where electric field effects are known to play a crucial role.

Manufacturing systems benefit significantly from the principles of Industry 4.0, particularly from the digital twin concept, which has a positive impact on job satisfaction when considered in conjunction with employee well-being. However, the widespread adoption of Industry 4.0 technologies has created new uncertainties for managers, which can be effectively managed by incorporating the concept of non-deterministic uncertainty into scheduling practices. This paper explores the application of two ambiguity metrics, known as $p$-center and $c$-center, for appointment-based scheduling under uncertainty. This approach is demonstrated using a real-world case study based on a manufacturing system, which showcases the effectiveness of the proposed method for handling uncertainty in scheduling.

Cyber-Physical Systems require a robust quality that enables them to withstand unexpected changes and function correctly, as opposed to being fragile and failing as a result. However, the concept of robustness lacks a precise definition, making it challenging to evaluate systems. This paper introduces a novel, formal approach to robustness, derived from temporal logic and control theory, that enables the quantification of robustness through a single, clear metric. This proposed method can be applied to systems that adhere to a STL specification and are subject to probabilistic disturbances. The potential benefits and feasibility of this framework are also discussed.

This study explores the potential of using accelerometer data to investigate
the presence of'shadow substances' within chemical containers. These substances
are not declared on the container label but are actually being stored. A key
feature of multi-axis accelerometer readings is their ability to distinguish
between live and empty objects. We demonstrate that this capability can be
utilized to identify instances where a container is being filled with a different
substance than what is declared on the label. A primary advantage of this
method is that it doesn't require users to have knowledge of the declared
substance. Moreover, since users are not required to provide any information
about the'shadow substance', the data collected remains completely anonymous.
A significant challenge arises from the fact that variations in user behavior can
affect the data. To mitigate this issue, our research introduces a data analysis
technique that can distinguish between different types of user behavior. This
approach involves utilizing a data reconstruction model to identify patterns
in data that are unlikely to be caused by user-induced changes. A preliminary
experiment was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of our method in
detecting'shadow substances'. The results show that when there are two types of
data patterns, one corresponding to live substances and the other to empty
containers, our reconstruction model can accurately identify the'shadow
substance' 80% of the time.

We investigate the local time delay resulting from the diffusion process on a curved, compact surface and create precise estimates for the approximation error in terms of a locally defined gradient. We also derive global gradient approximations for the diffusion process on a curved, compact surface and establish the rates at which they converge.

Radio sources in the extragalactic sky exhibit a broad range of brightness levels, 
from the faintest, unresolved sources to the brightest quasars. The characteristics 
of these sources have been studied through a stacking technique of radio maps at 1.4 GHz, 
utilizing data from the FIRST survey. The sources were categorized based on their flux density 
into three groups: quasars with a flux density greater than 1 Jy, sources between 0.3-1 Jy, and faint sources below 0.3 Jy. 
The sources within each group were further divided into sub-samples based on their angular size, 
ranging from less than 1 arcminute to greater than 3 arcminutes. The sources were analyzed for their 
morphological characteristics, using measures of asymmetry and kurtosis. The results indicate that 
sources below 0.3 Jy exhibit more pronounced asymmetry and higher kurtosis compared to brighter sources, 
suggesting a transition in their physical nature. The sources also appear to be more linear at smaller angular scales, 
which may be due to the effects of scattering. The data is consistent with sources below 0.3 Jy being primarily jetted sources, 
while those above this threshold are likely dominated by beam-jets or core-jets.

Statistical analysis of data flow can be a complex task, especially in systems with unpredictable behavior.  A novel approach to understanding data flow is offered through the use of a mathematical tool, the abstract concealed stochastic process.  This concept is based on a special type of mathematical framework, the abstract interpretation framework.  By applying a particular approach within this framework, data flow can be viewed as the outcome of a series of simple, monadic transformations.  This method is capable of accurately modeling both the rules-based behavior of software and the inherent unpredictability of random events.  As a result, it provides a unified way to express the interactions between these factors, even in cases where there is limited available data.  The effectiveness of this tool is demonstrated through its application to two real-world data sets, one related to malware traffic and the other involving web traffic.  In the case of malware traffic, the model successfully identified a previously known online malware campaign, as well as several other suspicious patterns.  In the case of web traffic, the model revealed a number of unusual patterns, including a significant number of requests to a particular website that is associated with malware, and a pattern of data transfer consistent with a known online fraud scheme.

This paper investigates the concept of information transmission within living systems, focusing on the inherent nonlocal characteristics arising from their dynamic consistency. It introduces a specific challenge posed by a system's ability to maintain dynamic consistency, requiring the transformation of local information into nonlocal information. The study establishes a mathematical framework for measuring a system's nonlocal capacity and provides an analytical expression for this measure in terms of the system's eigenvalues. It then demonstrates how to utilize an orthogonal basis to study nonlocality within linear systems, apply the concept to biological and psychological systems, and finally, discusses the implications of nonlocality for understanding the intricate nature of living systems.

We introduce a versatile framework for flexible scattering events in model-independent effective field theories, allowing for the incorporation of scattering cross-sections into collider-based new physics searches at a high degree of precision. This framework accounts for the impact of higher-order terms in the scattering process and provides a systematic expansion for the differential cross-section, ensuring internal consistency up to a specified order. We demonstrate the framework's effectiveness in generating accurate scattering amplitudes and cross-products for various processes, including resonant and non-resonant events. Additionally, we show the framework's compatibility with existing event generators like MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO and its ability to seamlessly interface with parton distribution functions.

A comprehensive analysis is provided for a blackbody in vacuum with strong external magnetic and electric fields, incorporating Casimir's effect. It is observed that the thermodynamic properties of the blackbody are influenced by the zero-point electric current, which originates from the interplay of the external fields and the quantized electromagnetic radiation. Specifically, the entropy of the blackbody is found to be unaffected by the external magnetic field, while it is dependent on the electric field via the anisotropic Van der Waals interaction associated with Casimir's effect.

This study investigates the relationship between a user's location privacy and the uncertainty of their predicted future locations. The user's privacy is quantified by the standard deviation of their estimated future positions, given their historical location data and an unknown movement model. The objective is to develop an optimal movement model that minimizes the standard deviation, thereby ensuring maximum location privacy. However, this issue is found to be insoluble, prompting the exploration of approximate solutions that either fix the movement model or fix the probability distribution of the user's future positions. The results demonstrate that an optimal probability distribution can be identified and used to compute a closed-form expression for the user's privacy, revealing that this is closely related to the weighted sum of the probabilities of their previous locations, where the weights are the estimated standard deviations of their future positions. The findings of this study are then applied to a real-world scenario, namely, the privacy preservation of users of ride-hailing services.

Locating objects within a 3D environment is crucial for numerous applications such as autonomous navigation, robotics, and geology. The emerging field of computer vision has given rise to data-driven approaches that surpass traditional methods based on kinematics. In this paper, we present a novel technique for point cloud localization using a transformer architecture that employs Normal Distribution Transform representation. The proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art solutions by leveraging a suitable point cloud description. The associated source code can be accessed on our GitHub repository.

A key challenge in brain connectivity research is identifying reliable connections between brain regions through resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). We investigated how to establish the existence of neural connections between spatially distant brain regions using multiple data sources. Our analysis of 1,000 pairs of regions in a dataset of 1,000 participants revealed that using long-duration data led to more robust connections. However, using shorter-duration data did provide more precise measurements of signal strength. We found that using long-duration data with a threshold of 10^-4 correlation coefficient led to optimal results, providing a strong statistical connection with high precision. Our approach is particularly useful for studying connections between regions that are far apart, with an anatomical distance of over 8 cm.

In a single-hop beeping network, nodes communicate with each other via a binary signal, and when two nodes start a conversation simultaneously, they enter a shared mode where they synchronize their beeping patterns. A consensus protocol is considered efficient if nodes reach agreement within a constant time and also minimize the overall beeping duration, and a new naming convention has been introduced that allows for a linear time agreement, while keeping beeping duration linear as well, and further research is being conducted to develop protocols that save power by limiting beeping duration through different naming techniques.

Code-mixed language speakers combine words from two languages in a single utterance, blending them in various ways. To improve understanding of code-mixed text, researchers have developed new methods, focusing on how words from each language interact. A key aspect of code-mixed language is the transition points where words from each language stop and start. To study this, a novel neural network, called PESTO, is presented, which uses a special way of representing words based on their position relative to these transition points. PESTO achieves good results on X-mix, a code-mixed language dataset, outperforming previous models, and demonstrates the importance of these transition points through intuitive visualizations.

The superconducting properties of H$_{3}$S are examined using a tight binding model that accounts for its electronic structure, incorporating the effect of van Hove singularities. The model's parameters are calibrated using the density of states and phonon-induced changes in the superconducting material's critical temperature are analyzed. The results show that the phonon-induced changes in the critical temperature are linear and can be combined with pressure-induced changes to explain the material's critical temperature, particularly its peak at high pressure. The calculated critical temperatures are in line with experimental results, suggesting that the material's superconducting properties are due to a combination of effects, rather than a single mechanism.

This study introduces a novel method for utilising motion planning data, specifically precomputed shortest paths, in dynamic environments where obstacles shift over time. The proposed approach, Spatial Restriction Creation, establishes temporal and spatial boundaries within which the state of the world remains consistent and the path can still be considered valid. The generated restrictions are then integrated with a path-planner to guide the system towards time-sensitive and obstacle-free motion. In experimental tests using a mobile robot, SRC outperformed alternative approaches, including a planner that adapts to changing conditions, by successfully avoiding obstacles along the planned path.

Visual navigation in challenging environments is crucial for robots operating in complex and dynamic settings, such as industrial facilities or search and rescue operations. The task of identifying visual landmarks in these scenarios can be difficult due to varying lighting conditions and feature degradation. The proposed approach utilizes 3D surfel maps to enhance visual relocalization by selecting suitable image features from preprocessed data. The learned features are then used to develop a probabilistic model, which estimates a robot's location by calculating the most likely pose given the observed data. The proposed method demonstrates improved performance compared to state-of-the-art techniques in both indoor and outdoor settings.

This paper addresses the problem of sparse signal recovery in multi-user MIMO networks through user selection and precoder design. To optimize performance, we focus on reducing interference among users by assigning weights in proportion to user distance and apply an innovative group LASSO technique for joint user selection and encoding. By incorporating user-specific encoding, we enhance the recovery of sparse signals. The proposed method is evaluated against existing techniques in both interference and noise metrics, demonstrating its superiority via simulations.

We demonstrate that the collection of logical function semifields associated with a fixed tropical curve has a finite basis, and this set can be expressed using elements from the semifield of tropical numbers over the underlying semifield. Additionally, for a tropical curve defined over a field with a finite cardinality, the collection of logical function semifields forms a vector space with a finite dimension.

In the context of linear regression, the Q-procedure is used to determine an optimal linear predictor by calculating a quadratic form of sample covariations between the dependent variable and its potential predictors. Consistent estimates in the form of sample means and covariates are commonly employed in place of their theoretical counterparts. This study investigates the asymptotic properties of the estimated Q-procedure across various scenarios. Notably, the behavior of the estimated Q-procedure is found to diverge significantly depending on whether or not the number of observations increases infinitely, and we find that the convergence rate is directly affected by the dimensionality of the estimates. Building on these findings, we suggest a modified version of the Q-procedure that is capable of achieving faster convergence rates through the use of data-purging techniques inspired by Bickel's approach.

A novel invariant, referred to as vark_3, is introduced which becomes trival under the operation of any ordered configuration of n-1, n, or n+1 points within the boundary of a 3-sphere. Furthermore, we establish that vark_3 can be represented as a Vassiliev 3rd order invariant through explicit construction.

The connection between unconventional superconductivity, antiferromagnetism and nematic order found in certain iron-based superconductors has sparked debate about the role of symmetry in superconducting materials. In the study of LiFeAs, a unique iron-based superconductor that becomes antiferromagnetic at extremely low temperatures, researchers investigated the potential link between its magnetic and structural transformations. By using advanced infrared spectroscopy, they discovered that the structural instability in the material is not as pronounced as in other iron-based superconductors and found that the structural phase transition in LiFeAs is not spontaneous, but rather can be induced by external pressure. This implies that the structural phase transition in LiFeAs is not as robust as previously thought and is overcome by the material's ability to become antiferromagnetic at low temperatures. As a result, the structural instability in LiFeAs is not as significant as in other iron-based superconductors, and further research is required to fully understand the relationship between its magnetic and structural properties.

This research focuses on a type of 2HDM known as the type-II variant, specifically the FR-II model, which shares similarities with the SM in certain sectors but differs in others. A crucial requirement for the model is that the second Higgs boson's mass must be greater than approximately 470 GeV. Our study investigates the possibility of adjusting the model's parameters to accommodate a measurement of 125 GeV Higgs boson's branching ratio for bottom quarks, which was reported to be consistent with the SM's prediction. We also analyzed the impact of experimentally measured values for Wilson coefficients related to the flavor changing process of neutral currents. These adjustments result in preferred regions for the model's parameters, specifically within the light second Higgs boson mass range and with moderate values for the non-hadronic contribution to the $\rho$ parameter. We then evaluated the model's performance under various constraints, including constraints related to flavor changing process of neutral currents and with moderate values for the non-hadronic contribution to the $\rho$ parameter. We also investigated the model's performance under different collider experiments, which could further restrict the model's parameters and potentially rule it out.

This research introduces innovative methods of self-assembly driven by a virtual neural network, where inorganic particles are programmed to work in harmony with organic neurons. We propose that these particles, termed neuro-procedures, can be defined as algorithmic instructions that integrate both organic and inorganic components. To achieve this, we employed neuroevolution, a process where a non-linear 'neural' model is developed through the combination of organic neurons and inorganic linear components. The integration of these elements enables the creation of complex, self-assembling patterns. We demonstrate this concept through the simulation of a simple 'target' task, where particles are programmed to assemble near a target point, showcasing the efficacy of our proposed algorithms.

We examine the dynamic development of anomalies in chiral gauge theories with an SU(N) gauge group, focusing on the impact of gauge boson mass terms induced through the Higgs mechanism. Our analysis reveals that these mass terms cause an SU(N) anomaly to form in the presence of N degenerate Higgs fields. This result holds even when the mass terms are introduced in a way that preserves SU(N) symmetry. We also investigate the development of anomalies in theories with non-Hermitian gauge symmetry, as well as those with explicit breaking of SU(N) symmetry. In contrast, theories with a broken SU(N) symmetry but preserved gauge symmetry do not produce anomalies. Our work provides a comprehensive understanding of the dynamic development of anomalies in chiral gauge theories and generalizes previous findings.

For three-dimensional, incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in a box domain, we've shown that if the Lp norm for p between 1 and infinity is controlled through the solution u to the steady NS equations, then the control is also applied to the initial condition f, with the control's size depending on the data's regularity and the exponent p. This result has been extended to the Cauchy problem of the heat equation, with similar conditions applied. These findings imply that the steady NS equations have a limited range of available initial conditions, specifically those within the Besov space with index p less than or equal to one-half, for the ill-posedness phenomenon to occur.

At extremely high pressures, certain materials undergo a phase transition from a dielectric state to a magnetic one. Researchers investigated how this transition affects the spin waves, or magnons, in these materials. They found that as pressure reaches its critical point, the energy gap associated with the magnons in these materials diminishes. As a result, the distribution of magnons changes significantly, leading to a shift in their average energy level. This shift is a consequence of the increased spin-spin interactions within the material. This research also revealed that this shift is more pronounced in materials with specific types of magnetic connections between neighboring spins. These findings demonstrate that the behavior of magnons in these materials is more complex than initially thought, even at extremely high pressures.

This paper introduces two modifications for enhancing the security of Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem. Originally constructed from Gabidulin codes, this system is vulnerable to several attacks. To improve its security, we propose modifying the key generation and decryption algorithms using matrix product codes. Specifically, we combine the matrix product of two maximal rank codes to create a pseudo-code with a high minimum distance, thereby providing a secure system. Our alterations are compatible with existing signature schemes as well as the current encryption protocol, and our computational experiments demonstrate their effectiveness in practice.

To enhance the effectiveness of pre-trained language models (PLMs), researchers have been exploring ways to utilize external dictionaries to infuse PLMs with domain-specific knowledge. This work proposes an innovative method for incorporating dictionaries into the BERT framework during the pre-training phase. By treating a dictionary as a hierarchical knowledge graph, we develop a knowledge propagation strategy that allows knowledge to flow from broader to more specific concepts, mirroring human cognition. Additionally, we create a knowledge retrieval mechanism that allows PLMs to access this external knowledge during the pre-training process. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed method's superiority on two datasets, with Dict-BERT models outperforming their non-dictionary-based counterparts.

In polytope algebra, a specific type of mathematical structure known as a bihomogeneous Hopf algebra has been established for studying continuous diagrams of geometric objects. By applying combinatorial principles to random polytopes in high-dimensional spaces, researchers have developed a corresponding algebra with similar properties. A key concept in this theory is the notion of a "minimal spanning acycle," which can be used to determine the volume of randomly selected polytopes. In this study, the researchers calculated the expected value of a particular component in the algebra when associated with a continuous diagram of minimal spanning acycles. They found that this expected value is directly proportional to the number of faces on the geometric shape, which is a characteristic known as the Euler-Poincaré characteristic, when considering a specific type of two-dimensional complex. Furthermore, the researchers applied their findings to a particular type of geometric shape and established a connection between the volume of its surface and the Euler-Poincaré characteristic.

In cross-referencing scenarios within a federated learning environment, a specific attack, referred to as a pragmatic privacy assault (PRA), exploits the differences in the security of the protocols used for member and aggregator operations. This particular attack specifically targets scenarios in which a certain percentage of participants may intentionally or unintentionally release sensitive information while participating in the learning process. We have identified and analyzed several PRA variants that utilize existing protocols such as Federated Learning, TFP, and ProtoSec, particularly highlighting how PRA can be applied in a vertical federated learning setup to compromise the security of an educational institution's data. We have further developed a new PRA variant, referred to as PRA-S, capable of extracting student ID information, demonstrating its potential impact on security.

A novel approach to dark matter inspired baryonic decays of B-mesons has been proposed, where a proton or neutron is accompanied by its antimatter counterpart. Research has focused on the specific decay process $B^+ \to p + \bar n^D$, with the heavy charm-meson part of the amplitude separated from the light baryonic component. Using QCD light-cone sum rules, the authors have quantitatively determined the latter's contribution and found it to be significantly smaller than the former's, except at excessively large momentum transfers. This finding implies that the light baryonic contribution is mainly responsible for the observed rate of the $B^+ \to p + \bar n^D$ decay process. Furthermore, the authors have applied their results to a specific dark matter model featuring a light hidden sector and found that the light baryonic contribution is essential to explaining certain anomalies in the $B^+ \to p + \bar n^D$ decay rates.

This research introduces the Intelligent Urban Defense Game, an innovative simulation tool for urban administrators to manage city resources during massive cyber-attacks that could cripple urban infrastructure. The defense system must allocate computing power, storage, and network capacity while fending off physical and cyber threats. Players must balance these efforts against the risk of accidental harm to innocent citizens from defensive operations. The simulation model is based on a game theory framework, incorporating a unique urban assault process and defense strategy, with a user-friendly interface and urban management game. Preliminary experiments demonstrate that human players outperform the current best AI algorithms in this task.

Researchers have discovered that certain universes with Casimir radiation exhibit unique phase transitions among black holes with negative, positive, and zero surface gravities. Using the brickwork method, they computationally determined the temperature of these black stars immersed in a cavity and found that Casimir radiation significantly impacts their behavior. Notably, the influence of the Casimir effect causes the black stars to undergo transitions at lower temperatures compared to those without the effect, and their temperatures can become positive under specific conditions, resulting in the restoration of thermal equilibrium. Furthermore, the study reveals that the thermodynamic properties of these black stars can be characterized by a Cyclic Path, consistent with the first law of thermodynamics.

Ranking algorithms play a crucial role in information retrieval systems by providing users with the most relevant search results. However, the performance of these algorithms is often hindered by noisy labels in the training data. To address this issue, we propose a method for correcting label noise in the context of article ranking, drawing inspiration from the process of retrieving physical documents. We develop a technique that involves selecting a batch of documents from a larger collection, both physically removed from the system and electronically removed from the index. This approach leads to the introduction of label noise, and we treat the remaining documents as positive examples, while the removed documents are considered negative examples. To improve training efficiency, we employ bag sampling, partitioning the positive batch into smaller groups. Additionally, we design a customized loss function that minimizes discrepancies within each group, and a unique objective function that maximizes the difference between positive and negative examples. Experimental results demonstrate that our method effectively corrects label noise and enhances the retrieval of articles ranked by the algorithms.

Recent advancements in GNN-based self-supervised learning have achieved remarkable performance without the need for labels. However, these methods often struggle when only a small number of labels are provided. To address this challenge, we propose IPS TAG, an innovative framework that utilizes pseudo-tagging to enhance self-supervised learning with limited labels. By integrating IPS, a state-of-the-art method that improves pseudo-label quality, and TAG, a technique that optimizes pseudo-label distribution, our framework produces more accurate and diverse pseudo labels. We then leverage these pseudo labels to refine the initial model, achieving better performance. Our framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on various datasets, outperforming existing approaches that utilize pseudo labels.

In linear accelerators of the form 2D-PIE, a plasma is used to increase the energy of particles of a specific shape. The AWAKE experiment at CERN aims to use this type of accelerator to accelerate 400 MeV protons and accelerate ions into the tens of GeV range. The acceleration occurs through the interaction of high-energy protons with spiral slices of plasma, where the energy transfer happens via the bunch's betatron oscillations. The increased energy is then transferred to the center of the bunch, which is subsequently accelerated by a strong electric field. The performance of the accelerator is limited by the energy loss of the electrons within the bunch due to the bunch's rapid oscillations. This type of energy loss has been analyzed in previous studies, but the actual performance of the bunch in AWAKE's second run has been analyzed in relation to the experiment's specific setup and plasma conditions.

To ensure the confidentiality of users participating in distributed machine learning, a novel method employing differential privacy has been developed for decision tree learning. This new method accounts for both the geometric constraints of decision trees and the specific requirements for maintaining differential privacy, resulting in an exact algorithm for private decision tree construction. To address the computational intensity of this method, an optimized version of the algorithm is presented, along with a method to enhance its efficiency through parallel processing at multiple scales. Experimental results demonstrate that the optimized algorithm can efficiently construct private decision trees, with the parallel version offering significant speed improvements. Notably, the research also reveals that existing private decision tree construction methods can result in substantial tree structure alterations, even with a relatively high level of privacy, whereas the optimized algorithm is able to minimize such changes effectively.

This study introduces a novel approach for inferring a probability density function (PDF) based solely on a target PDF and a distance metric, specifically the R\'enyi distance. The proposed method leverages advanced optimization techniques to enhance the method's performance and versatility. The method's effectiveness on a variety of numerical examples demonstrates its ability to handle a range of parameters, from small to very large datasets. The proposed method is further compared to existing PDF inference methods, showcasing its superior accuracy and efficiency.

Network modeling through the Chain Event Networks (CEN) approach has proven effective in analyzing complex event sequences. CEN models are composed of discrete time intervals and interconnected events, allowing for a comprehensive analysis of dependencies between single events. However, determining the optimal model parameters, specifically the number and duration of time intervals, remains a significant challenge. This study presents a novel Bayesian approach to automatically select time slots for CEN models. The proposed method utilizes a Bayesian information criterion to identify the optimal model parameters without prior knowledge of the network structure. The framework integrates Poisson process assumptions to accurately model event frequency within selected time slots. The proposed method demonstrates comparable accuracy in network reconstruction as existing techniques but with the added benefit of objective framework selection.

This paper explores the convergence properties of a Damped Inertial Tikhonov regularization method applied to weakly convex and locally Lipschitz optimization problems. Notably, when the objective function has a particular structure, consisting of a convex component and a smooth, non-differentiable part, it is possible to establish asymptotic convergence towards the Minimal Norm solution even in the presence of vanishing Tikhonov regularization. To achieve this, a Damped Inertial Tikhonov regularization scheme is designed, which effectively unifies the core minimization problem and the Tikhonov penalty in a single, consolidated equation. Building on this framework, it is possible to demonstrate the convergence properties of the method when the regularization parameter approaches zero.

A group of autonomous, boundary-following robots is studied under the influence of a unique, time-varying communication network. Each robot receives a signal based on the average from its neighboring robots and adjusts its speed to maintain a set distance from the next closest robot in its vicinity. The collective behavior of these robots is the focus, with the analysis revealing that even simple robots can exhibit complex behavior, including sudden and unexpected shifts in trajectory. The results show that these shifts can arise from a stable equilibrium point, characterized by two distinct, self-repeating patterns over different time scales. The emergence of this stable point is determined by specific conditions in the robots' initial setup, leading to a two-part classification system based on the robots' initial configuration.

Within the framework of the Hubbard-EE model, we have investigated the microwave conductivity in superconducting state of the Hubbard-EE model with disordered kinetic energy, focusing on the impact of doping, energy gap, and frequency of the electromagnetic field. Our findings reveal that the energy gap in the superconducting state diminishes with rising kinetic energy disorder but increases with the density of charge carriers. The microwave conductivity is influenced by the kinetic energy disorder and undergoes a shift in frequency in the vicinity of the Hubbard model's critical point. The microwave conductivity is also found to be affected by the binding energy of quasiparticles and exhibits a significant increase in high-frequency microwaves with rising kinetic energy disorder and increasing binding energy of quasiparticles.

This article provides an overview of recent developments in crystalline-like movement, focusing on the part of the crystal that experiences positive and negative curvature. It explores a variety of results, including the establishment of mean curvature motion for small pieces of the crystal and the development of motion based on integrated curvature. Additionally, the article discusses the connection between movement driven by integrated curvature and the movement of planar crystals driven by anisotropic surface energies. Furthermore, the article discusses the challenges associated with defining a motion that is based on average curvature and presents initial results in this area.

This paper introduces GrowSpace, an innovative system that utilizes top-down shape capture data to guide plant development in optimal ways through targeted adjustments to growing conditions. GrowSpace empowers users to define a target plant morphology and then automatically generates customized temporal sequences of environmental factors, like light and temperature, to shape the plant's growth in accordance with their specifications. GrowSpace's effectiveness is demonstrated through successful applications in training compact trees to serve as space-saving architectural elements and in creating unique, naturally-wired plants for decorative purposes.

We present a novel approach to the stochastic Levy process that describes random conformal deformations of a simply connected domain. This approach is based on the concept of conformal equivalence, resulting in a non-Markovian process, which can be represented as the outcome of a sequence of independent random variables, each associated with a specific partition of a domain. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between these random variables and the Radon-Nikodym derivative in the context of the Loewner-Kufner-Regularity equation, which governs the growth of a certain type of growing region. Additionally, we provide an in-depth analysis of the process in the specific case where the domain in question is the entire complex plane, leading to a characterization of the process as the solution to a specific class of partial differential equations, which includes the Liouville equation as a particular instance.

The widespread adoption of open-source software has accelerated the pace of progress in data analysis, but its lack of standardization has led to a contradictory effect, hindering collaboration among researchers. In the field of image analysis, the proliferation of new software has created a multitude of formats for representing results, often in an non-interoperable manner. In response, a diverse group of experts has come together to establish the Image Indicator Standardization initiative, aiming to develop and promote open, platform-independent standards for encoding images and their metadata. The proposed standards will facilitate seamless communication among images and databases, fueling advancements in data visualization, machine learning, single-cell analysis, and other areas, and ultimately contributing to the advancement of image-based research as a whole.

The inclusion of high-spin nucleon and delta resonances explains the observed spectrum of nucleon and delta resonances and aligns with isospin symmetry, resulting in a good fit for $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ photoproduction data.

Determining the authenticity of bionic faces, created through expert manipulation, typically involves a few steps: initial data extraction, refinement of the facial structure, identification of key features, and comparison with real faces. However, the initial step is critical, as it directly influences the accuracy of subsequent processes. This study focuses on the first stage of an algorithm designed to detect synthetic human faces by comparing them with authentic ones. The proposed method utilizes a combination of OpenCV techniques to apply a standardized processing routine to a large dataset of faces. The chosen methods include histogram equalization, de-noising, and filtering to correct color inconsistencies, remove noise, and fill in gaps, respectively. The study's findings indicate that these operations can effectively restore degraded images and correct errors in a large dataset of faces.

This study presents novel solutions to several longstanding cosmological and astrophysical problems, including how to achieve a matter-dominated universe, the cosmological baryon asymmetry, and the formation of supermassive, ancient black holes. Our approach suggests that the curvaton, rather than contributing to dark matter, was the primary source of energy density in the early universe. The generated perturbations led to black hole formation, and subsequent non-linear interactions caused the curvaton to decay into stable, negatively charged particles. This process resolved the cosmological baryon asymmetry, and the formation of these particles also explains the dominance of dark matter by protons. Furthermore, we propose that the early black holes, such as Sgr A*, have cores composed of stable, charged particles rather than bare protons, and that their event horizons are surrounded by a cloud of negatively charged particles. This model predicts that the radio emission from these regions could be responsible for the radio quiet, luminous centers observed in our galaxy and M87.

Higher education institutions strive to enhance their academic programs by making informed decisions about course offerings, leading to a significant need for effective analysis tools that can accurately depict students' study habits. To address this challenge, we have developed a novel application of a specific statistical model that can accurately reconstruct students' educational journey. Building on the existing framework of academic pathway models, we have adapted and refined the model to better capture students' course enrollment patterns. Furthermore, our approach incorporates a strategy to assess model fit and evaluate the consistency of students' educational trajectories. The proposed method has been successfully applied to actual data sets, resulting in a high level of reconstructed pathway accuracy among the existing methods, at 93%.

To address the growing issue of traffic, researchers are exploring the application of evolutionary principles to manage the flow of vehicles. This study proposes a new approach to regulate traffic patterns by leveraging the principles of the reproductive strategy known as differential contests. This method involves vehicles participating in a contest-based game that adjusts their speed according to intervehicle distance, leading to self-organizing patterns that minimize real-world traffic challenges. Our model demonstrates that under specific conditions, the system converges to stable equilibrium states, characterized by consistent headway distances and out-of-phase velocity patterns. These patterns are similar to those observed in real-world vehicle platoons, which have been shown to reduce traffic congestion and improve safety. Our approach offers a scalable and efficient solution to regulate traffic, as it does not rely on centralized control and can be implemented using advanced technologies such as linked and automated vehicles.

In this paper, we examine the dependency between the two logistic regressions $f$, $g$ when their outputs share the same input $x$. This unique investigation leads to an unexpected finding: when functions $f$ and $g$ are drawn from an infinite and uniform distribution, the minimum number of samples $N$ required to detect this dependency can be calculated using the formula $N \approx \frac{1}{\delta^2} \sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{3}}$. Notably, our result diverges from the commonly applied $\sqrt{\frac{N}{\delta^2}}$ due to its inaccurate assumption of independent samples. To address this issue, we propose a novel dependency test, referred to as the "differential empirical covariance test," which effectively circumvents the interaction between the two functions by utilizing a specific type of differential covariance. Furthermore, our empirical analysis demonstrates the test's efficiency in real-world scenarios, including its application in the context of two-party computation, where we observe a significant reduction in samples needed, averaging around $25\%$ of the expected minimum required for uniform distribution draws.

The proliferation of social media has led to an explosion in text-based data, fueling the development of advanced natural language processing (NLP) systems. One area where NLP systems have excelled is automatic headline creation, and this capability has been eagerly adopted by data scientists and NLP practitioners. This paper examines the effectiveness of cutting-edge transformer architectures, particularly BERT and XLNet, in recognizing automatically generated headlines. Our study draws from the Grounded Semantic Recognition Datasets, which provide a foundation for grounded language understanding. Our findings demonstrate that transformer-based models can achieve impressive results, and we also investigate the benefits of incorporating domain-specific knowledge to enhance our detection capabilities.

A comprehensive study of the magnetic properties of MnSi, a unique helimagnet over a broad range of temperatures and pressures, is conducted. At low pressures, the material exhibits antiferromagnetic order at very low temperatures and a chiral spin fluid within a specific temperature interval where it displays re-entrant helical order. Our research focuses on how the chiral spin fluid forms at higher pressures by examining the material's magnetic phase diagram. At low pressures, the chiral spin fluid arises from the competition between disorder and magnetic order, and as pressure increases, the boundaries between crystalline and amorphous phases become blurred. Ultimately, the material transitions into a state where it exhibits polycrystalline characteristics before reaching a point where it behaves like a single, uniform crystal.

The increasing popularity of large-scale radio interferometers, exemplified by the SKA project, has led to a pressing need for efficient calibration methods to manage the computational demands associated with these instruments. Traditional calibration techniques have been inadequate for the large-N, high-resolution imaging requirements of next-generation radio interferometers. To address this challenge, we have developed and implemented an innovative calibration framework, leveraging matrix representation and singular value decomposition to transform the complex calibration problem into a reduced-dimensional data analysis task. Our method, combined with a novel singular value thresholding strategy, enables accurate calibration even in the presence of noise. Notably, the computational complexity of our approach is characterized by a linear relationship with the number of antennas involved, thereby circumventing the computational bottlenecks inherent in traditional methods.

In investment management, the principle of diversification is crucial for minimizing potential losses. This study proposes a novel approach to creating investment portfolios that effectively diversify risks. Leveraging recent advancements in deep learning frameworks, we have developed a risk diversification recommendation system. This system utilizes a conditional generative adversarial network model to generate synthetic and implicit portfolio compositions for a given pool of assets. By training a discriminator as an autoencoder, we can evaluate the diversity of generated portfolios relative to the original asset pool. This enables the system to identify underutilized assets and output recommendations in the form of relative investment allocations. Our model's effectiveness was validated through a numerical case study using historical price data of 11 US stocks over a 3-year period.

We have established the polarized transition matrix components $A$ for quark flavor changes in QCD at the next-to-next-to-leading order through their full set of integrals. This achievement allows us to simplify the calculation of the polarized structure function $g_1$ and the associated anomalous dimension through the use of the massless and massive variable flavor collision method at the next-to-leading, leading, and next-to-leading orders for four, three, and two active flavors, respectively.

We utilize a Bayesian neural network, an advanced form of convolutional neural network, to analyze a dataset of 824 gamma-ray active galactic nuclei (AGN) from the Fermi Large Area Telescope. Our analysis focuses on classifying the AGN into two categories based on their 3 GHz radio luminosity: a high radio luminosity group of starburst-driven AGN and a low radio luminosity group of jet-driven AGN. We train the Bayesian neural network on a separate dataset and apply it to make predictions for the entire sample. Our results show that the Bayesian neural network is able to accurately classify the AGN, with 83% of the sample's classification matching the labels of the training data. We also investigate the potential for systematic errors in the classification and find that the Bayesian neural network is less susceptible to these errors compared to other machine learning methods.

Despite numerous benefits, the number of content creators on social media remains limited due to several barriers, particularly for individuals with disabilities. To encourage more people to become creators, researchers must investigate the challenges creators face and develop strategies to overcome them. This study focuses on social media accessibility from a content creation perspective, examining the obstacles and opportunities related to accessibility features. Through a survey of 13-to 16-year-old public platform users, we identified key challenges, including a lack of accessible content options, inconsistent accessibility features, and limited user control over accessibility. However, we also found that users appreciate inclusive language, clear instructions, and varied content formats. Based on our findings, we offer practical recommendations for social media platforms to enhance content creation accessibility and encourage more users to become creators.

A general approach is established for calculating the spectrum of a hypergraph, specifically its Laplacian matrix, by combining multiple hypergraphs. This methodology has practical applications in studying the mixing times of random random walks on hypergraphs. The proposed method is initially demonstrated through an analysis of the spectrum of two hypergraphs, which is then expanded to accommodate any finite collection of hypergraphs. This technique is exemplified by calculating the spectrum of the tensor product of two hypergraphs, which is also analyzed for specific cases, including the tensor product of two complete 3-dimensional tensors.

A space-based telescope with a 2-meter aperture is proposed, featuring an extensive range of spectroscopic and imaging capabilities. This includes a wavelength range from 0.4 to 5.0 micrometers with various observational modes. A comprehensive overview of the INSIST mission and instrument framework highlights its potential for groundbreaking scientific discoveries and serves as a foundation for further discussions on the mission's details and costs.

To accurately assess the progression of Alzheimer's disease in clinical trials, we develop a novel method to measure treatment group differences over time using a smooth, curvaceous curve. This approach, inspired by data from the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale, leverages a type of smooth function called a natural cubic spline. Our analysis, performed through Monte Carlo simulations and case studies, demonstrates that this method can detect treatment group differences better than traditional repeated-measures ANOVA. Additionally, we apply our approach to examine the differences between donepezil and placebo in two actual clinical trials.

In the field of chemistry, nuclear physics, and materials science, identifying transition paths between states or structures is a critical issue. We propose a novel, universal method to discover the most common transition routes for achieving a state or structure by globally enhancing actions, which involve incrementally improving a trial configuration in the direction of a target state or structure through geometric optimization. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through its successful application in guiding quantum chemical calculations and simulating nuclear shell movements. Compared to other methods, this method can reduce the number of required calculations, in some cases by factors of thousands to ones. Additionally, we found that our transition path predictions for hexagonal to cubic phase transitions in rocksalt divanadyl phosphate using density functional theory closely align with experimental results and those obtained through other methods.

We establish the existence of uniformly bounded solutions for a class of parabolic equations, including complex Monge-Ampere and Hessian equations, under prescribed boundary and initial conditions, thereby proving the stability of these systems' metrics/Hessian metrics. Building upon this result, we show that a version of the mean-value property holds for these uniformly bounded solutions.

In the context of regular classes of functions, one particular class stands out for its strong properties: CE, which corresponds to the $\lambda$-calculus's untyped $\lambda$-recursion. Interestingly, when we move to the realm of typing, things become more nuanced. The class CE is still attainable, yet other notable function classes, such as EX and HY, remain unreachabe through typed means. However, a recent breakthrough by M. Escardó in 2008 revealed that a typed analogue of the sacking process does indeed correspond to the class HY. This paper aims to expand upon that finding by proving that a typed version of Mitsuhi's operator, which is known to generate HY, successfully produces functions within the same, distinct class HY.

The paper explores the relationship between Ito and Stratonovich integrals when the integrand has varying parameters, derived from a specific type of stochastic process called conditional distribution flows. These flows are based on a Brownian motion with a specific condition. The paper establishes a key result, showing that a unique Ito process can be created from a conditioned Brownian motion. Additionally, it proves a crucial equivalence between conditional flows and their Ito integrals, similar to Ito's formula. This equivalence shows that a conditional flow can be represented in two ways, either as an Ito integral or a Stratonovich integral. The paper also introduces a method to determine the relationship between Ito and Stratonovich integrals, based on a specific correction term. This correction term can be used to convert Ito integrals into Stratonovich integrals and vice versa.

In an earlier work, we established a two-part topology on the set of subgroups within a locally compact Hausdorff group, consisting of the topological isomorphisms and the subgroup topology derived from the original group. We found that adding a weight less than or equal to $\aleph_1$ to this set of subgroups results in homeomorphic standard structure spaces in all cases. We further established that a group $G$ has a compact subgroup structure if and only if it has a compact Hausdorff locally compact scale, provided the group's cardinality is less than or equal to $\aleph_1$.

This study addresses the challenge of text-to-SQL parsing in databases lacking a schema. A primary issue with current approaches is that they often generate invalid queries due to a lack of understanding about database constraints. To tackle this problem, researchers propose a new parsing task called "meaningful parsing", focusing on generating code that adheres to database integrity constraints in addition to standard parsing. The proposed task requires parsing models to incorporate multiple output formats. To alleviate the difficulty in obtaining annotated data for this task, a data augmentation technique is designed to convert existing annotations into relevant ones. The research further demonstrates that producing meaningful parsing can be beneficial with minimal supervision. The experiments conducted on the Spider dataset reveal that the proposed approach leads to improved performance in both exact match and follow-up questions. The research was performed on the Spider dataset, a benchmark for text-to-SQL parsing in the absence of a database schema. The results indicate that the proposed parsing method outperforms previous models in both tasks.

This paper presents a model predictive framework for collaborative robot navigation that prioritizes security. The proposed approach builds on a previously developed model, incorporating a convex risk-averse formulation to account for uncertainty. To mitigate computational complexity, a data-driven optimization framework is developed, utilizing generative adversarial networks to simulate probability distributions and reduce processing time. The efficacy of this model is demonstrated through simulations of multiple robots navigating diverse environments, yielding substantial improvements in computational efficiency. The proposed framework also effectively balances security and efficiency, as illustrated by the analysis of risk and performance metrics.

Our research on Andromeda XXV, the smallest and densest dwarf spheroidal discovered by the Pan-Andromeda Archaeological Survey, reveals it to be a low-mass galaxy with a mass of 1.1 billion solar masses. Using VLT data, we analyzed the velocity dispersion of Andromeda XXV and found it to be 4.3 km/s per square arcsecond, equivalent to a velocity dispersion of 5.1 km/s. By combining this information with the galaxy's projected half-light radius of 23.1 parsecs, we estimated the central surface brightness of Andromeda XXV. Our analysis revealed a lack of significant gas or stellar content within the galaxy, suggesting that Andromeda XXV is primarily composed of dark matter. Using the mass-to-light ratio derived from the mass and velocity dispersion, we calculated the luminosity of Andromeda XXV in solar units. Our results show that the luminosity of Andromeda XXV is approximately 1.8 times 10 to the 4 solar units. Our research further indicates that the ratio of Andromeda XXV's dark matter to total mass is 0.85, or 85 percent.
