A new approach is proposed for extracting detailed information from time-based data, particularly in molecular dynamics, where the focus is on a single molecule. This method builds upon a previously established forward-modeling framework and incorporates an optimization technique to refine initial guesses. By iteratively applying this procedure, it is possible to achieve stable and robust convergence of the model without overfitting, even when initial assumptions are inaccurate. This proposed method is demonstrated through analysis of time-based data from single-molecule spectroscopy experiments, where it successfully determines the rates of individual spectroscopic events. Furthermore, it is shown that this approach can accurately reproduce time-based trajectories and retain the level of detail present in the original data.

Recent developments in autonomous driving have seen significant advancements driven by large, open-source datasets. The availability of such resources has enabled the creation of increasingly accurate and reliable self-driving car models. Current datasets, however, primarily focus on camera-based views, neglecting other essential aspects of naturalistic driving. To address this, we've introduced SceNDD, a comprehensive dataset designed to capture the complexities of natural driving scenarios. This dataset combines multi-camera, sensor data with contextual information, including vehicle kinematics, to provide a more complete picture of driving environments. The development of SceNDD involved collecting over 100,000 seconds of data from real-world driving scenarios, carefully curated to include a diverse range of situations. We've also developed a novel method for training agent policies using this data, leveraging the contextual information to optimize performance. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of SceNDD in enhancing agent capabilities and its potential to contribute to the ongoing autonomous driving research community.

This paper explores how reflected entropy, a concept within holographic quantum gravity models, can be reinterpreted within the framework of conformal field theories in boundary/interface settings. Firstly, we express reflected entropy in terms of the entanglement wedge cross-sectional volume. Subsequently, we apply the Ryu-Takayanagi formula to connect reflected entropy to the geometric characteristics of a specific probe shape in a two-dimensional black hole environment. Our findings reveal that reflected entropy is directly related to the geometric attributes of the probe, specifically the area of its cross-sectional volume. Moreover, we establish a correlation between entropy rate and the probe's minimum width. These connections between reflected entropy and geometric characteristics are also evident in the context of random surfaces. Notably, our research shows that reflected entropy can be expressed as a specific version of the Fishnet diagram virtual algebraic degree of a polynomial, a concept that has been extensively studied in the context of holographic quantum gravity models.

In our research, we have developed an efficient RIS-assisted OFDM system with enhanced channel estimation capabilities. The model takes into consideration the limitations imposed by incomplete pilot symbols and inaccurate hardware representations within the RIS. To overcome these challenges, we have devised an effective least squares-based estimation method, which is subsequently supported by an advanced sparse Bayesian inference approach to address the noise issue. To further improve estimation accuracy, we have developed a sophisticated iterative least squares-based sparse Bayesian inference technique. Notably, our study also introduces an innovative sparse domain sparse Bayesian inference method to counter the adverse effects of hardware malfunctions. Theoretical performance evaluations are conducted, followed by an analysis of the computational complexity of the proposed algorithms. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed methods yield substantial gains in terms of signal-to-error ratio improvements.

We examine the connection between two key concepts, the non-invasive measurement approach and the individual energy fluctuation theorem. The non-invasive measurement approach is significant in statistical mechanics as it provides a method to calculate system energy based on observable properties. The individual energy fluctuation theorem, proposed by us, is a generalised version of the Jarzynski equality and provides a method to calculate the thermal energy of a system. We demonstrate that an individual energy assessment according to the fluctuation theorem is achievable for integrals of motion, and that this assessment is equivalent to a non-invasive measurement. We also show that any thermal cycle conducted on a system at equilibrium, and in a confined environment, can be expressed as a combination of individual energy assessments.

We investigate the deformation theory of G2-instantons on a 7-dimensional Riemannian manifold with a nearly G2 structure. The union of these manifolds with G2 structure forms a Lie groupoid, allowing us to apply the Lusztig-Janezica theorem to the deformation space. The space of infinitesimal deformations is captured by a cohomology group, while the deformations themselves constitute a representation of the zero-section's 1-jet deformation group. The deformation space can be identified with a finite-dimensional abelian Lie group, depending on the second cohomology group with coefficients in the unitary group U7. The existence of an open dense subgroup further confirms the deformation space's Lie group properties.

The COVID-19 pandemic, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, has become a global health crisis, prompting governments to implement a variety of measures to mitigate its spread. In Brazil, a national contact tracing system was established to monitor the virus's progression, with the goal of reducing its fatality rate. This system, based on location data, uses machine learning algorithms to identify at-risk individuals. However, concerns have been raised regarding the confidentiality of users within Brazil's COVID-19 contact tracing framework. This paper aims to address these concerns by examining the security of this system, with a particular focus on its first version, known as Coronav\'irus-SUS. This application, linked to the national health database, uses location data provided by mobile phone manufacturers to identify close contacts. However, a vulnerability was discovered, enabling unauthorized access to user location data. This paper outlines the vulnerability and proposes a solution to enhance the system's confidentiality.

High-performing deep neural networks rely heavily on input data, particularly in complex tasks such as image recognition, where significant amounts of carefully labeled data are required to achieve optimal results. However, standard deep neural networks operate within a fixed data framework, which is inherently classical and fixed in size. This limits the potential for networks to process and learn from vast amounts of quantum data, a key feature of many emerging technologies such as quantum sensors and quantum communication systems. To address this limitation, researchers are developing quantum data structures that enable efficient representation and management of quantum data, facilitating tasks like data enhancement, feature extraction, and model training. This study explores the principles and current implementations of quantum data structures in deep neural networks, including both foundational and cutting-edge approaches.

This research paper introduces a tool for automatically translating ACL2 representations of C code into executable C code and verifying their correctness through the use of ACL2 theorems. 

A custom, ACL2-specific embedding of C code structures and functions the user inputs is analyzed and abstractly represented within ACL2's environment. 

A proof-generating C code generation framework is developed to produce C code that corresponds to ACL2 functions and interacts with representations of C variables. 

User-defined ACL2 functions of a specific form can be used to specify how these representations translate to C code, without needing to modify the underlying logic frameworks or implement any new decision procedures. 

This framework is demonstrated by embedding a selection of ACL2 rational number functions into a C-like logic and proving its effectiveness through a series of ACL2 theorems that validate the generated C code's correctness.

A comprehensive study of the (39991) Iochroma asteroid family's orbital dynamics has been conducted to understand its formation history. Our research utilized a semi-analytical approach, incorporating various factors such as the YORP torque, collisional statistics, and thermally relaxed equilibrium shapes for its parent body. We discovered that the YORP vector's time evolution is consistent with observations of the Iochroma family. By analyzing the semi-analytical results, we determined that the Iochroma family likely originated from a parent body with a diameter of approximately 20-25 km. Our research also revealed that the Iochroma family's YORP vector is consistent with its observed C-type spectral characteristics. However, a detailed simulation of the YORP vector's time evolution is required to confirm this correlation.

Building upon Ramanujan's finding that $\zeta(2n-1)$ is expressible as a linear combination of odd zeta values of lower magnitude, this work develops an analogous result for a particular generalization of the Hurwitz zeta function.

We demonstrate in this note that the equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces constructed from finite-dimensional complex vector spaces V is given by the graded elliptic cohomology module generated by 1, provided that translations in the complex and the dual of the vector space V, as well as the action of the circle group, are all accounted for. This establishment is grounded in the identification of a key long exact sequence.

The rapidly evolving connection between machine learning and the mathematical tools of topology is generating significant interest across various fields of science. This emerging trend is driven by the prospect of applying topological concepts to describe intricate phenomena in physics. The intersection of machine learning and the mathematical tools of your parents' discipline is an exciting development that may hold the key to understanding complex systems in physics. In this review, we explore the applications of machine learning topological concepts in physics, discussing recent advances in the area. The applications of machine learning topological concepts in physics are diverse and promising. The intersection of machine learning and the mathematical tools of your parents' discipline is an exciting development that may hold the key to understanding complex systems in physics. Recent advances in the area are diverse and promising.

Calculations of the $J/\psi + \eta_c$ and $J/\psi + \chi_{cJ}$ processes at next-to-leading order are carried out to assess whether observed deviations from predicted angular distributions can clarify the $J/\psi + \eta_c$ anomaly. These calculations involve including all significant diagrams and using the $^3S_1^{[4]} \to ^3S_1^{[4]}$ transition process for $J/\psi$ decays. Following the release of Belle's revised data on $J/\psi$ angular distributions, an investigation was conducted to see if any of the $J/\psi$ production mechanisms could be responsible for the $\sin^2\theta_{J/\psi}$ deviations. These calculations show that none of the $J/\psi$ production mechanisms can account for the observed anomalies.

Our study examined the understanding of personal PINs among Signal users, categorizing them as "secure" PINs intended for encryption and "casual" PINs used for convenience, as well as a subset of "secure" PINs meant to be shared. We conducted online surveys with 1,000 users, classifying them into "enthusiasts" based on their level of engagement with Signal and the presence of additional security measures. Our analysis revealed that 28% of all users had guessed their PINs, with 17% having done so among "enthusiasts". Notably, 22% of users without a guessed PIN had attempted to reset it, with 15% doing so among "enthusiasts". We found that "casual" PIN users were more likely to have guessed their PINs and attempted to reset it compared to "secure" PIN users. Our study also showed that "enthusiasts" who used "secure" PINs were less likely to have guessed them and attempted to reset them.

This study presents a novel solar-weighted Gaussian quadrature rule designed to efficiently compute solar energy for functions of the form $f(x)\phi(x)S_x^k$, where $\phi(x)$ represents band edge functions, $S_x^k$ signifies power-law functions with exponents $k$, and $f(x)$ is a real-valued function combining band edge and power-law factors. The proposed method offers precise integration within specified error limits, whereas conventional methods like Monte Carlo integration provide approximate results with specified precision. The method's accuracy and efficiency are demonstrated through successful solar energy integration for various semiconductor materials, including silicon, germanium, gallium arsenide, and tungsten, resulting in accurate and precise integration rules for these materials.

The second-order optimization method's efficiency in deep learning is hindered by the computational expense of the Hessian matrix and its inverse. The Hessian's curvature properties are often approximated through the Fisher Information matrix or the Gauss-Newton matrix. Our research reveals that a standard neural network's optimization can be represented as a function of a generalized Gauss-Newton matrix, which encompasses the Fisher and Newton matrices as special cases. By analyzing the low-dimensional structure of this matrix, we develop an efficient technique to calculate the curvature, making higher-order optimization in deep learning computationally feasible for the first time. Our method accurately predicts critical points, allows for the identification of unstable points, and facilitates the identification of local and global minima. The ViViT structure, which enables the efficient computation of the generalized Gauss-Newton matrix, is a key component of our method.

This study explores how grammatical gender influences word representations in languages that assign gender to nouns. We've found that in these languages, words related to the same gender often cluster together in vector space. We've analyzed data from three languages - Spanish, German, and Greek - and discovered that our method, using only co-occurrence counts, accurately predicted gender for most words in these languages. Our research also reveals that gender stereotypes are embedded in the word representations of these languages.

A group is considered charmable if it can be generated by 2 nilpotent subgroups, and our study focuses on the charmability of finite groups. Our research reveals that any group G with a charmable quotient group, and a 2-generated p-socle, also has its derived subgroup charmable. Furthermore, this result leads to implications for the charactertistic 0 case, and we provide examples of finite groups that satisfy these conditions. Additionally, our study extends the concept of charmability to nilpotent groups and includes applications to the hyperbolic plane and nilpotent algebras.

Estimating the position of objects within an image is a complex task that involves both object detection and localization. In our study, we explored an enhanced version of zero-shot object detection that focuses on determining objects' positions. We discovered that utilizing the same detection model that was trained for detection tasks results in poorly accurate localization. In contrast, employing a separate model specifically trained for localization yields more reliable outcomes. Notably, even using an ideal detection model, object localization remains a challenging task. We analyzed the underlying causes of this difficulty and found that object features tend to be more stable than background features, which makes the localization task more intricate. We also examined the effects of image resolution, object types, and scene complexity, revealing that certain environmental factors can simplify the localization task.

Predicting future traffic conditions is crucial for city planners and drivers, and it's a challenging task. Existing short-term traffic forecasting models often rely on sparse and irregular data, which limits their effectiveness. To tackle this issue, we've developed a new approach that combines traffic flow measurements with spatial and temporal characteristics. This approach identifies key features - such as traffic density - by analyzing the similarities between nearby locations over time. By applying this approach, we can improve the accuracy of traffic forecasting even with limited data, and it outperforms existing models in this area.

This study introduces VACA, a social network platform allowing users to share variational graph neural network (GNN) models for making causal inferences. These models can be utilized for analyzing the effects of specific interventions on network data and evaluating counterfactual scenarios. Users can leverage VACA to compare the performance of different models on various tasks, such as estimating causal effects and identifying key nodes for targeted interventions. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of VACA as well as three case studies demonstrating its capabilities.

The ongoing expansion of radio interferometers is significantly influencing the study of transient radio sources. A crucial area of research within this field is the detection and identification of Fast Radio Bursts and other transient events. A newly established system at the Irish LOFAR station is being utilized to test and refine real-time data processing techniques, including the detection of these enigmatic FRBs. Comprising 12 high-density antennas, the LOFAR station's advanced capabilities enable the collection of high-resolution data in a relatively short timeframe. A key component of the system is the integration of the HEAVEN pipeline, which is responsible for processing and analyzing raw data in real-time. Preliminary results from the combined system are presented, including a notable single-pulse detection with a 5-sigma significance.

Metamaterials receive significant attention in the field of photonics due to their ability to manipulate light behavior through the combination of carefully designed structures that attribute unusual optical properties. Recent advancements in civil metamaterials have been facilitated by their simplicity and cost-effectiveness, allowing for mass production and potential integration with standard manufacturing techniques. This article reviews the developments in civil metamaterials, highlighting their types, advantages, and applications. Additionally, it discusses how artificial intelligence and machine learning approaches have been utilized to design and optimize civil metamaterials.

The successful filmmaking industry relies heavily on film analysis to determine which movies to invest in, where studios assess the potential earnings of upcoming films based on factors like genre, production company, and box office predecessors. Researchers working to improve film analysis tools have access to a limited number of films, making it difficult to achieve comprehensive understanding. To address this limitation, a larger film dataset was compiled, spanning 75 years, from 1940 to 2015, with a focus on identifying key attributes that influence box office revenue. The proposed method involves combining film characteristics prior to release with existing features and using linear regression to model and predict gross income. The results indicate that the new approach significantly enhances film analysis, resulting in a 10% increase in predictive accuracy.

The integration of vast amounts of renewable energy capacity has given rise to a pressing need for the efficient management of energy systems in terms of frequency regulation. Due to their inherent intermittent nature, a significant proportion of renewable energy generation must be complemented by large-scale capacity, which is typically achieved through the installation of large wind turbines. However, these turbines are incapable of providing frequency regulation. To address this challenge, researchers have proposed innovative solutions, such as the use of smart inverters, auxiliary power control methods, and the integration of flywheel energy storage systems. Nonetheless, existing solutions are often limited by constraints in communication, leading to difficulties in practical implementation. In light of this, a novel approach has been developed to stabilize voltages without relying on communication, by leveraging the inherent capabilities of smart inverters. Specifically, inverter capacity can be utilized to modulate its real and reactive power outputs, thereby modulating the inverter's impedance and angle. Consequently, the inverter's influence on the surrounding network is extended beyond its immediate vicinity, enabling the stabilization of voltages through adjustments to real and reactive power. Notably, this approach is capable of providing both primary and secondary frequency regulation, as well as maintaining voltage stability across various scenarios.

This research introduces a new class of highly intelligent cyberphysical systems, specifically networks of autonomous agents that can perceive their surroundings and make data-driven decisions. The focus is on systems with cognitive capabilities, achieved through advanced data analysis and artificial intelligence. The proposed framework models these intelligent networks and their functioning through a dual-cognitive approach, incorporating two key layers: a perception layer and a reasoning layer. The perception layer is responsible for data extraction, filtering, and feature selection, while the reasoning layer performs complex analysis and makes informed decisions. The study also investigates the cognitive capabilities of these networks through a framework for knowledge representation and artificial intelligence, demonstrated by two real-world applications showcasing their potential.

This research explores the extension of holomorphic functions over complex spaces with irregular surfaces, applying techniques from hyperbolic geometry and topological structure, and demonstrates an extension theorem for functions that are close to being bounded on such spaces, and proves a related theorem for pseudoconvex domains that share specific properties.

We investigate the difficulty of detecting two identical, pure states in a multi-partite system. Our analysis shows that in certain cases, these states can be virtually detected without any accompanying calibration measurements. This phenomenon occurs when a specific, symmetric property is inherent to the states and associated measurement operators. We provide general conditions under which N-particle systems can virtually detect these states, and demonstrate these conditions with specific examples.

A theoretical model based on the concept of quantized splintering of strings offers an explanation for baryon formation. Utilizing the Abelian dominance approach associated with the confinement phenomenon, our analysis focuses on a specific type of string configuration known as a "helicoid". This particular configuration is characterized by three color loops linked together, forming a loop-in-loop pattern, which gives rise to a baryon-like state. Notably, breaking this configuration results in the creation of a baryon, accompanied by gluons and quarks. This theoretical framework is applied to various baryon states, including $\Lambda$, $\Sigma$, $\Xi$ and $\Omega-$ hyperons. By quantitatively analyzing the helicoid configurations associated with these baryons, our study reveals that string splintering energies align with the masses of these baryon states.

The time it takes for seismic waves to travel from the surface to a deeper layer, as observed using helioseismology, has shown an unexpected increase over the past four years. This rise in time intervals cannot be fully explained by changes in the Sun's surface temperature or rotation speed. We investigated whether variations in the Sun's active regions, particularly in the circulation of energy, could contribute to the observed time changes. Our analysis focused on the impact of currents around active regions and used simulations to assess their potential effect on the Sun's interior. We discovered that currents surrounding active regions can significantly affect the Sun's deeper layers and, as a result, influence north-south travel-time measurements. This discovery explains a substantial portion of the observed time changes and highlights the importance of considering the Sun's active regions and their dynamics when analyzing the Sun's interior using helioseismology.

Gravitational waves emitted by cosmic strings can be detected within pulsar radii through the periodic oscillations of extremely old and strong magnetic fields. These intense magnetic remnants from the early universe could have been created during a phase where magnetic flux conservation was violated. Early universe magnetic fields may have been responsible for the large-scale magnetic phenomena observed in our cosmos, such as magnetic alignment and large-scale magnetic fields. If the gravitational wave signal from these ancient magnetic fields is detectable before the next decade, it could provide significant insights into the early universe, such as its evolution of EoS for matter, the properties of primordial black holes and the characteristics of the early cosmic magnetic fields.

Light field technology has shown promise in various applications, with its inherent ability to restore and refocus images being a major advantage. However, capturing and processing light field data at high resolution is computationally expensive due to its massive size, making efficient compression techniques crucial. In this research, a practical approach to light field image compression is presented, incorporating insights from learning algorithms. A novel model called DC-EP is introduced, which integrates the connections between disparity maps and light field images to improve compression efficiency. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through experimental comparisons with existing compression techniques in terms of multiple criteria, including rate-distortion performance, image quality, and processing efficiency.

Cross-language information retrieval is a complex task that involves retrieving relevant documents based on a query in a different language. One of the primary challenges in CLIR arises when users are unable to express their queries in the search language, leading to the field being divided into two distinct frameworks: interactive and non-interactive. In the interactive framework, queries are generated through query selection and query formation processes, while the non-interactive framework involves translating queries in a single stage. Despite their individual strengths, these two frameworks have coexisted for decades, each addressing different aspects of the CLIR challenge. However, recent advancements in deep learning techniques have allowed for the development of integrated and combined approaches that harness the benefits of both frameworks.

Small-area estimations are crucial in low and middle-income countries as surveys are often underrepresented in vulnerable regions. This study compares traditional approaches used in high-income countries to a simpler method developed by the World Bank. The results show that the new method outperforms the old ones, providing more accurate results. The study also suggests ways to improve small-area estimations in low and middle-income countries.

We've developed a new approach to implementing the Kelly betting strategy within a quantum computing framework, suitable for both continuous and discrete variables. This strategy is designed to optimize portfolio growth by minimizing its lower bound's rate of decrease in a fair market. Our approach utilizes a two-qubit entangled resource, represented by the Bell state |∅⟩, to create a superposition |ψ⟩, which is used to generate a random number through measurement, serving as a virtual random number generator. This random number is then used to place bets in the original (discrete) Monrath model. Our results indicate that wagering with the quantum resource, when based on the Bell state |∅⟩, yields a growth rate identical to the optimal outcome when using truly random numbers, generated via the quantum bit commitment (QBC) protocol. Furthermore, we've discovered that utilizing the W state |W⟩, in place of |∅⟩, results in a growth rate slightly lower than optimal, yet still superior to that achieved with classical random numbers. Our research demonstrates that quantum resources can be leveraged to produce outcomes at least as good as, and potentially superior to, those achieved with true random numbers, as dictated by the principles of quantum mechanics.

The two-dimensional semiconducting single-layer moissanite, specifically the MASP family with transition metals (M = Mo, W, Ti), has garnered significant interest due to its exceptional optical and electrical properties. By employing advanced computational methods, researchers have conducted an in-depth analysis of moissanite's electronic structure and stacking-dependent variations across different structures. The study reveals a unique alignment between the semiconducting single-layer and the quasiparticle-gapped superconducting bilayer forms, regardless of the stacking arrangement. The findings suggest that the system's electronic properties are influenced by a common stacking-independent exciton state, potentially explaining the consistent excitonic features observed in different structures. The study's outcomes have significant implications for the development of advanced moissanite-based optoelectronic devices.

The investigation of the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay provides valuable insights into the $\Sigma^-$ baryon's properties, as its mass can be determined by measuring the decay rate of a $\Sigma^- $ baryon, whereas the $\Lambda$ baryon's properties are studied through the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay at the LHCb experiment. The experiment has observed $6.1 \sigma$ evidence for the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay, with an observed frequency of $2.44 \times 10^{-8}$, and has predicted a future discovery of $5.55 \times 10^{-8}$ with the increased data set from 20~fb$^{-1}$.

A theoretical model for the formation and evolution of protoplanetary disks is introduced, based on the collapse of a prestellar core. The proposed model starts with the core's center shrinking under gravity, eventually transforming into a prestellar nucleus. The surrounding material then begins to fall onto this central point, forming a protoplanetary disk. The model's development from core collapse to disk formation is similar to the core's evolution, with the central pressure increasing and the material density decreasing. The resulting protoplanetary disk features an inner region with high pressure and high temperatures, where small particles cannot survive, giving rise to a gap in the disk and separating it into inner and outer regions. The model suggests that the gas giants in a system will form within this inner high-pressure region, with rocky bodies and asteroids potentially inhabiting the outer disk area.

High-resolution imaging of celestial objects in the near-infrared and mid-infrared is hindered by atmospheric turbulence. To rectify this issue, ground-based telescopes use various techniques such as adaptive optics, but these methods are ineffective without accurate 3D models of the atmosphere. Unfortunately, current computational simulations of atmospheric turbulence are not grounded in empirical evidence. To bridge this gap, researchers have conducted on-site observations of atmospheric turbulence using high-resolution data from the IOTA telescope, capturing detailed snapshots of the atmosphere at 10 millisecond intervals. These observations reveal complex 3D structures, including layers of uniform temperature and varying humidity levels. Notably, the data show that atmospheric dynamics are most intense near the ground, but also exhibit significant mid-level activity. These findings have been used to develop a set of standardized 3D atmospheric models, each representing different scenarios, such as standard conditions and scenarios with intense turbulence.

Long-term forecasting in complex systems is a difficult task due to the limitations of current models, which are typically designed to handle short-term sequences. We propose a new approach called multi-term temporal sequence modeling, where we analyze extended versions of popular models, such as LSTM and GRU, to improve long-term forecasting capabilities. We observe that these models often fail to utilize all the available data, leading to incomplete information. To address this issue, we developed a novel method to incorporate sparsity into our approach, which is based on a non-local energy function and a Gibbs distribution. We used a state-of-the-art Bayesian variational inference technique to train our model, which allows it to learn the optimal parameters. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, which significantly outperforms existing models by leveraging sparsity and capturing long-term patterns.

This note outlines a continuous reasoning approach to understanding Pontryagin duality and using the dualities of topological groups to solve equations in the form of the map $p:X\to Y$ being continuous if and only if the corresponding map $p^*: \widehat{Y}\to \widehat{X}\) is a homeomorphism. The article also explores the utility of Pontryagin duality in solving equations involving maps of compact sets and proves that the equation $p:X\to Y$ having a solution if and only if the corresponding map $p^*: \widehat{Y}\to \widehat{X}$ is continuous is a key concept in the field.

The primary advantage of federated learning is that it allows a model to be trained on user devices without collecting their personal data, thereby protecting user privacy. However, this benefit is not extended to the selection of the training parameters, as the choice of hyperparameters, such as batch size, is made centrally and applied uniformly to all participants. In this paper, we introduce a novel, local computation-based approach to selecting federated learning batches, referred to as Local-FedBatch, which aims to replicate the performance of the traditional, centralised method using smaller sample sizes. Building on this concept, we propose an adaptive learning strategy that adjusts the batch size in response to the statistical characteristics of the data, thereby improving model convergence while maintaining participant privacy.

A proposed supersymmetric $U(1)_X$ model, with $R$-parity broken, offers an alternative to natural SUSY models. This model features a hidden $U(1)_X$ gauge sector with three generations of $SU(2)$-triplets at the TeV scale. As a result, the $U(1)_X$ gauge sector is naturally connected to dark matter and dark energy. We examine the model's potential to explain the observed neutrino oscillation indications, the baryon asymmetry of the universe, the abundance of dark matter, and the universe's present-day dark energy state. We also investigate the model's capacity to generate the necessary Fayet-Iliopoulos term for SUSY $U(1)_X$ gauge sector stability.

This research presents a novel approach to improve the throughput of an IRS-assisted wireless network that harnesses energy using an unsupervised learning method. The main objective of this network is to facilitate simultaneous communication and energy harvesting between a transmitter, receiver, IRS, and an eavesdropper. To achieve this goal, we devised an IRS reflecting surface optimization method that maximizes the signal-to-interference power ratio. Notably, the presence of the eavesdropper in this setup introduces a complex problem involving a non-convex objective function under discrete constraints. To address this challenge, we leveraged an unsupervised learning method to convert the non-convex problem into a convex one with continuous constraints. The implementation details of this method are provided, and its efficacy is demonstrated through comprehensive simulations that show a substantial improvement in throughput compared to conventional IRS-assisted systems.

For the first time, researchers have studied the beta-plus decay performance of $^{186}$Hg using the IGISOL particle accelerator. The decay's Gamow-Teller strength distribution for the $7/2^{-}$ isospin transfer was measured for the $^{186}$Hg to $^{186}$Tl transition. A maximum of $10.1\pm0.3_{stat}\pm0.8_{sys}$ units of relative strength was recorded for the initial 77% component of the decay, which matches theoretical nuclear structure models. This finding helps to validate the theoretical models of the $^{186}$Hg beta-plus decay and its implications for the study of nuclei near the proton-neutron-dense region.

Within the framework of low-energy desert supersymmetry, a unified model was developed that incorporates all features. The model successfully addresses several issues at the electroweak scale, including the origin of dark matter, baryon asymmetry, rare lepton decays, neutrino masses, and constraints related to the Higgs mass and dark radiation. The implementation of a'semi-direct' gauge mediation method for supersymmetry breaking and low-scale gauge coupling unification enabled model parameterization. The model predicts a 'f-atmospheric' neutrino mass pattern, rare $\mu \to e$ transition, a Higgsino-dominated dark matter composition with a predicted dark matter relic abundance, and a predicted value for the effective number of neutrino species, $\delta N_\nu$.

In the field of robotics, researchers face a significant challenge: creating algorithms that can effectively control complex systems with limited data availability. To address this issue, they propose a new method called the Multi-Task Trajectory Matcher, which uses a small dataset of expert trajectories to teach the controller how to navigate complex systems. The proposed controller learns a universal trajectory representation that can be applied across different systems, even with limited data. Notably, this approach enables a single controller to successfully operate on various robots with different designs, simply by providing a new dataset of reference trajectories. The Multi-Task Trajectory Matcher is tested on a simulated aircraft with an onboard computer, demonstrating its ability to learn and adapt within a short time span of 10 minutes.

The Toda conformal quantum field theory based on the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ simple Lie algebra has a distinct characteristic where it unifies the Toda field with higher spin fields through Ward relations. This is similar to the behavior observed in the Toda conformal quantum field theory based on the $\mathfrak{osp}_{2n+2}$ simple Lie algebra. This theory has a unique action on the space of local observables, which includes the Toda field and higher spin fields. This action is determined by the Virasoro algebra and Kowalski-Gleason and Ruelle's higher spin currents. These currents are derived from the algebraic structure of the Toda conformal quantum field theory and are shown to satisfy a bootstrap equation. This equation is a consequence of the integrability of the Toda conformal quantum field theory. This theory is characterized by the presence of a two-component fermionic current that plays a crucial role in deriving the Ward relations. This current is used to express the Toda field in terms of the higher spin fields. This expression is a consequence of the Toda conformal quantum field theory's classical action principle. This principle is a consequence of the integrability of the Toda conformal quantum field theory.

We introduce Relation Generative Adversarial Networks (RelGAN), an innovative model that utilizes a connection network to learn a latent space where a GAN can generate high-quality real images. RelGAN achieves this by mapping input images to a unified feature space, where a discriminator can identify authentic images. Our design builds upon the connection network architecture of Inception net, and incorporates a triplet loss to ensure that the learned features are distinct and unique. RelGAN has been successfully applied to various applications such as unsupervised domain adaptation, and our experiments confirm its superior performance in this area.

A new approach to twin-field quantum key exchange has been developed, eliminating the need to synchronize phases. The phase-free TFQK protocol relies on unitary operations along with a specific encoding strategy to create entangled states, allowing for key exchange without requiring phase synchronization via public communication channels. The phase-free TFQK protocol achieves identical key rates as the standard TFQK protocol and offers increased efficiency due to reduced need for public channel use in practical implementations.

Let $\phi$ be a non-negative function on a one-dimensional complex space with derivatives that increase moderately and compactly supported, and consider the Toeplitz algebra generated by specific Toeplitz operators on Fock and Bergman domains with symbol $\phi$. This algebra can also be represented as a subalgebra of $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{F}_\phi)$, the algebra of bounded linear operators on the weighted Fock space with weight $e^{\phi}$. Similarly, it can be represented as a subalgebra of $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{B}_\phi)$, the algebra of bounded linear operators on the weighted Bergman space with weight $e^{-\phi}$. This representation implies that the Toeplitz algebra is closed due to its being contained within the commutant of an orthogonal projection. This containment is proven by first establishing that certain Toeplitz operators with symbol $e^{\phi}$ are compact, and second, that the Bergman and Fock projections have compact inverses on L^2.

In recent years, lexical knowledge has played a crucial role in advancing various NLP tasks, but its incorporation into vision and vision-language tasks has been limited due to the labor-intensive process of curating visual lexicons. To address this challenge, we introduce OpenLexico, a large-scale visual lexicon comprising over 40,000 words with high-quality image embeddings derived from a pre-trained model. To enhance the accuracy of OpenLexico's word representations, we developed a novel technique that leverages pseudo annotations obtained from user-generated data on social media platforms. Specifically, we employed a neural bounding-box prediction model to refine OpenLexico's word embeddings by treating the word representations as pseudo annotations. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, as the word embeddings generated with pseudo annotations outperform those generated without them.

The research involves a detailed analysis of the cloud's radio continuum and line emissions, as well as Hubble Space Telescope data, to understand gas dynamics. The research also found that a large-scale outflow is likely driven by a young star in the cloud.
